cards.f: Paper 2 Section A: what is the task?
cards.b: Compulsory. Read two texts on one topic and write an argumentative or discursive letter, article or speech, 250-350 words.

cards.f: Which two bullet points are always asked?
cards.b: Evaluate the ideas in both texts, and give your own views.
Judge how strong, fair, reliable or convincing an idea is, not just report it.
Report: 'Text A says homework helps.' Evaluate: 'Text A's only evidence is one teacher's experience, so it is weak.'
What evidence? Is the writer biased? Is it exaggerated or one-sided? Does it apply to everyone?
Evaluates ideas from both texts thoroughly, reads between lines, combines ideas into a developed argument.
Summarising Text A then Text B with no judgement.
Address the audience, state the issue and your overall position.
Opening, body 1 (ideas evaluated), body 2 (opposing ideas evaluated), body 3 (own view), conclusion.

cards.f: Register for a letter to a headteacher?
Register for a school magazine article?
cards.b: Semi-formal, lively, with a headline and engaging opening.
'The writer claims..., yet offers little evidence...'.

cards.f: Why must you use both texts?
cards.b: Using only one text limits the reading mark.

short.q: Explain the difference between reporting and evaluating. [2]
short.model: Reporting says what a text claims. Evaluating judges how strong or convincing it is, e.g. by considering evidence or bias.

short.q: State two questions to ask when evaluating an idea. [2]
short.model: Is there enough evidence? Could the writer be biased?

short.q: What should the opening paragraph include? [3]
short.model: Address the audience, state the issue and give your overall position.

short.q: Why is a clear overall position important? [2]
short.model: It gives the answer a focused argument, and avoids changing position without explanation.

short.q: Why does summarising each text in turn limit marks? [2]
short.model: It shows no judgement. Top levels need evaluation and a developed argument.
